Action Plan:
1) Schedule and perform a comprehensive neurological examination with dilated fundoscopy via the clinic’s support line; proceed with the examination as soon as feasible; if headache resolves, the visit can be cancelled.
2) Initiate pharmacologic management for acute headache: prescribe a stronger NSAID alternative to ibuprofen (dose/route/frequency not documented) and continue/paracetamol as needed (dose/route/frequency not documented); counsel to take both medications with food.
3) Arrange follow-up and safety monitoring: plan to check blood pressure at the appointment and review ongoing use of combined oral contraceptive pills in the context of migrainous features; escalate to imaging or specialty referral if red flags or persistent/worsening symptoms develop.
4) Referrals and escalation: if examination indicates, pursue neurology/migraine specialty referral; book appointment with support team to facilitate a full examination.
5) Patient education and red-flag guidance: provide instructions to seek urgent care (A&E) if headache worsens, new neurologic deficits emerge, fever develops, or there is any new convincing change in symptoms.
6) Documentation and consent: ensure verbal consent for transcription and documentation of plans; verify adherence to take medications with food.

Subjective:
- Chief complaint: New, severe, disabling headache for 3 days; interferes with work and concentration.
- Onset and course: Abrupt onset upon waking 3 days ago; constant since onset; partial relief with ibuprofen but not resolved; currently persistent.
- Location and quality: Headache described as all over with focal emphasis around the right eye.
- Associated symptoms: Photophobia; light sensitivity; occasional flashing/shooting visual phenomena; mild nausea; no vomiting; no fever; no neck stiffness; no focal weakness, numbness, or speech difficulties.
- Intensity: Pain rated around 8/10 at peak, down to ~5 with some relief.
- Night symptoms: Sleep is generally OK; not waking from headaches at night; may wake with headache in the morning.
- Triggers/positional factors: Brief stabbing pain with rapid head movements or quick standing.
- Eye/vision: Recent eye examination reported no changes in vision.
- Respiratory/ENT symptoms: No cough, sore throat, nasal symptoms; no sinus pain.
- General: No significant weight change; fatigue may be related to ongoing headache.
- Medications: Oral combined contraceptive pill (started ~1 year ago); ibuprofen as needed; paracetamol not routinely used prior to this visit.
- Allergies: None.
- Social history: Lives alone; works from home; drinks alcohol about once per week; non-smoker.
- Family history: Mother has migraines.
- Relevant past medical history: Prior childhood headaches; one short episode about 2 days long that resolved with ibuprofen; no chronic headaches reported since; no known drug allergies.
- Recent health checks: Blood pressure reportedly normal when checked in pharmacy about a year ago (during OCP use); no fever and no systemic signs.

Objective:
- Not documented in real-time during this visit; planned actions include a full neurological examination and fundoscopy.
- Symptom-focused observations noted in history: photophobia, light-triggered symptoms, right-eye–predominant pain, visual phenomena (flashes/shooting lights).
- Eye exam history: recent normal eye examination with no vision changes reported.

Assessment & Plan:
1. New-onset, persistent headache with features suggestive of migraine (likely migraine with aura or migraine without aura with photophobia):
   - Assessment: Migraine-type headache is the leading consideration given photophobia, visual phenomena, unilateral emphasis, family history, and partial NSAID response.
   - Differentials consistent with the transcript and DDx (supporting evidence): migraine with aura (high likelihood); CVST risk related to estrogen-containing OCP (medium likelihood); idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) (medium likelihood); intracranial mass (low likelihood); meningitis/encephalitis (low likelihood).
   - Investigations planned: Comprehensive neurological examination; dilated fundoscopy during visit; consider imaging (MRI/MRV) or further workup if red flags appear or symptoms persist/worsen.
   - Treatment planned: Stronger NSAID alternative for acute relief (dose/route/frequency not documented) plus paracetamol as needed (dose/route/frequency not documented); take with food.
   - Referrals: Schedule full examination via clinic support line; neurology/migraine specialty referral to be considered after examination if indicated.
   - Safety/when to seek urgent care: If headaches worsen, new focal neuro deficits develop, fever, or any concerning change, go to A&E.

2. Contraception considerations (related to migraine features and OCP use):
   - Assessment: OCP use may influence migraine patterns; ongoing evaluation needed.
   - Plan: Blood pressure check at the appointment; review OCP suitability in the context of migrainous symptoms; if migrainous features persist or worsen, discuss possible switch to an alternative contraception method.

3. Follow-up and ongoing management:
   - Plan: Book appointment with support line for full examination; monitor symptoms; adjust management as needed based on exam results.
   - Education: Continue meds as prescribed with food; monitor headache pattern and triggers; return sooner if red flags appear.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing elements: No documented current vitals (BP, pulse, temperature), no current neurological exam findings, no imaging results yet, no formal medication reconciliation beyond patient-reported meds.
- Internal conflicts between transcript and DDx: None identified; DDx includes several plausible etiologies consistent with history; no direct conflict noted. (conflict noted: none)
- Transcript quality: Generally adequate; some brief inaudible segments during the call, but core history and plan are clear.

Additional notes:
